name: Agent Database Access and Permissions
title: Agent Database Access and Permissions
answer: Agent database access and permissions covers the question of what an AI agent is allowed to read or change when it queries a database on someone's behalf. When an agent queries a database for a user, it should see only what that user may see. Row level security, scoped credentials, read only roles and audit logging are the controls that keep an agent from becoming a way around existing permissions. The topic sits at the join of AI and SQL, and it matters most wherever an agent is wired to a live production database rather than a copy.

sections.body: Agent database access and permissions covers the question of what an AI agent is allowed to read or change when it queries a database on someone's behalf. When an agent queries a database for a user, it should see only what that user may see. Row level security, scoped credentials, read only roles and audit logging are the controls that keep an agent from becoming a way around existing permissions. The topic sits at the join of AI and SQL, and it matters most wherever an agent is wired to a live production database rather than a copy.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The plumbing is usually a database connection exposed to the agent through a tool interface, most often a Model Context Protocol server. This site currently tracks 2,569 active Model Context Protocol servers, 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses, which shows how common that pattern has become. Underneath, the agent holds some credential, whether a shared service account, a per user token, or a short lived session, and that choice decides almost everything about what it can reach. The database itself does the rest of the work through roles, views and policies.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: In practice the work is done by pushing the permission decision down into the database rather than trusting the agent to filter results. Row level security policies keyed to the acting user, read only roles for anything exploratory, and views that expose only approved columns are the usual building blocks. The agent's queries are then generated against that constrained surface, and every statement is written to an audit log with the user, the session and the SQL text. Teams test the setup by replaying queries as different users and checking that the rows returned match what those users could see directly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The rights and risk side turns on provenance and accountability. If an agent reads data through a shared credential, the audit trail shows the agent and not the person, which breaks the link between access and identity that most policies assume. Scoped credentials, per user sessions and logging that records both the requesting user and the agent preserve that link. Data protection rules, contractual limits on the data, and internal access reviews all still apply, and an agent does not create an exemption from any of them. This page describes practice only and is not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward identity that follows the user all the way through the agent, with short lived tokens, policy expressed once and enforced at the database, and logs that can answer who saw what. As more SQL servers appear in the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, the interesting work is less about connecting an agent to a database and more about proving that the connection respects the permissions already in place. Expect the controls to consolidate around the database engine rather than around each agent framework.
